name: Secular height trend

card.summary: The long-run rise in average adult height across generations, which looksmaxxers cite to explain why environment (nutrition, health) shapes height and why growth-stage factors matter for how tall someone ends up.

quick.overview:
The secular height trend is the documented rise in average height from one generation to the next in many countries, seen in military conscript records, passport files and national child-growth surveys. In height-focused communities it is used as a reference point for how much of final height is set by environment (diet, illness, living conditions) rather than genes alone.

Research reviews attribute the gains mainly to improved nutrition, health and social conditions. Studies from Switzerland, Sardinia, Japan, South Korea and China show gains of several centimetres over decades, with slowing in some wealthy populations.
quick.how: People use the idea as context rather than as a technique: it frames why childhood and adolescent nutrition, sleep, illness and puberty timing are discussed in height threads, and why population growth charts are periodically updated.
quick.risks: There are no direct risks, since it is a population observation. Researchers caution that average trends say little about any one person's height, and that rising height in some countries has coincided with rising body weight.

lead: The secular height trend is the increase in average adult height across successive birth cohorts, documented in many countries since the 19th century. In European countries, rates of roughly 10-30 mm per decade have been reported.[5] It is studied through military conscript records, passport and convict registers, and national child-growth surveys.[1][2][3]

In looksmaxxing and height-focused communities the trend is cited as evidence that height responds to environment: nutrition, infection burden and general living conditions during growth. Anyone interested in maximising height therefore tends to focus on growth-period factors such as diet, sleep and puberty timing, as this is where population gains have been attributed.

A literature review concluded that the positive trend can be attributed mainly to improvements in health, economic and social conditions, and that reported rates vary by age, socioeconomic status and country.[1] Encyclopedic summaries note that height gains in industrialised countries of up to about 10 cm over roughly 150 years have largely levelled off.[10]

chain: Better nutrition, health and living conditions in childhood
Fuller expression of genetic growth potential
Taller average adult height across generations
angle.text: The trend shows that growth-period environment shifts adult height by several centimetres at population level. Height-focused communities use this as the rationale for attention to childhood and adolescent nutrition, sleep and health, which are the factors credited with the gains.

paras: Secular trends are changes in a biological measure across generations. For height, the trend means that people born later are on average taller than those born earlier in the same population. Differences tend to be larger in childhood than adulthood because maturation also advances, and trends are not apparent before about age two.[5]

Pre-industrial and Neolithic skeletal evidence suggests no large height differences from the Neolithic until the early 1800s, apart from a decline associated with the shift to agriculture, according to a summary on Wikipedia.[10]

Swiss conscripts aged 19 grew on average 14.9 cm between 1878-79 and 2009, reaching 178.2 cm in 2009.[7] A study of passport, convict and army-auxiliary records found the trend in males from the 1870s/1880s birth cohorts and in females from the 1840s/1850s.[3]
Sardinian conscripts gained 6.77 cm between 1883 and 1986 (about 0.66 cm per decade), with much faster gains of 2.39 cm per decade between cohorts born in 1948-49 and 1964-68.[2]

Japanese and South Korean children became appreciably taller over about fifty years, with larger changes in South Korea; most of the adult height increment had already accrued by about 1.5 years of age, and the growth period advanced in timing and shortened.[4] In China, national surveys 1985-2015 showed rapid growth gains, with urban children surpassing WHO 2006 standards by 2015 and the trend slowing in the last decade.[6]

World War II slowed the trend in several countries, with stronger gains after the war than early in the century.[1] Wikipedia notes the Dutch, among the tallest populations, have been reported to have stopped growing taller.[10]

Reviews attribute the trend to environmental influences, particularly nutrition, health and social conditions.[1][5] Protein quality, meat, dairy, eggs and fish intake are linked with taller average heights in encyclopedic summaries, and famine and malnutrition with stunting.[10] A comparison of North and South Korean cohorts is cited as an example of the size of the nutrition effect.[10]

Some researchers have also modelled whether height-selective migration could contribute to apparent trends in spatial networks, although the simulations did not fully match Swiss conscript data.[8] Selection and measurement bias in recruit data is another recognised caution.[9]

Height discussion communities refer to the trend when arguing that diet, sleep and health in the growth years matter, and that genetics sets a range rather than a fixed outcome. It is also used when comparing heights between countries and generations.

The evidence is population-level rather than interventional. Cohort and survey studies across Switzerland, Sardinia, Japan, South Korea and China describe the trend, and reviews summarise its drivers.[1][2][4][6][7] No clinical trial has tested the trend itself, since it is a population observation.

timeline.event: Female (1840s/50s) and male (1870s/80s) height gains begin in Swiss birth cohorts.[3]
Swiss conscript records begin the series showing a 14.9 cm rise by 2009.[7]
Peak gains of up to 3.67 cm per decade in Sardinian cohorts.[2]
Chinese national surveys record rapid growth gains, slowing in urban children.[6]
